Distribution-First Framework for Learning Risk-Sensitive Individualized Treatment Rules

Zhen Fang Affiliation: Department of Statistics and Operations Research Affiliation: University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill Email: zhenfang@unc.edu    Guanting Chen Affiliation: Department of Statistics and Operations Research Affiliation: University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill Email: guanting@unc.edu    Yufeng Liu Affiliation: Department of Statistics Affiliation: University of Michigan Email: yufliu@umich.edu
Abstract

Learning a risk-sensitive individualized treatment rule (ITR) with patient covariates is challenging when the treatment criterion depends on the full conditional outcome distribution rather than only its conditional mean. Existing methods are largely criterion-specific, making it difficult to compare multiple treatment criteria within a common pipeline, such as quantiles, conditional value-at-risk (CVaR), and complex preference-based objectives such as cumulative prospect theory. We propose a distribution-first framework for risk-sensitive ITR learning that first estimates treatment-specific conditional outcome distributions and then constructs the target ITR by plug-in criterion evaluation. The proposed framework unifies treatment rule learning across multiple criteria and accommodates hard-to-optimize objectives within the same estimation pipeline. On the theoretical side, it yields a general error propagation result for locally Hölder-stable criteria, linking first-stage distribution estimation error to downstream criterion estimation and treatment regret, together with sharper regret bounds under standard margin conditions. Empirically, we show that the proposed framework outperforms direct criterion-specific methods in multiple settings and further evaluate it on the ACTG175 HIV clinical trial, a randomized study comparing several antiretroviral regimens in HIV-infected adults.

1 Introduction

Personalized decision making is a central goal in precision medicine, aiming to move beyond the traditional “one size fits all” paradigm and tailor treatment decisions to patient-specific characteristics [1]. A core statistical approach to this problem is learning an individualized treatment rule (ITR), which maps patient covariates to treatment recommendations to optimize a clinically meaningful objective. Over the past two decades, a rich literature has developed around optimal ITR learning, including regression-based and value-based approaches that seek treatment rules with the best expected outcome, leading to substantial progress in individualized treatment learning [2, 3, 4, 5, 6].

In many treatment decisions, however, the conditional mean alone does not fully reflect what matters clinically. Two treatments may have similar expected outcomes but substantially different lower-tail behavior, variability, or asymmetry, leading to different risk–benefit profiles for different patients. This limitation has motivated growing interest in risk-sensitive treatment criteria that depend on distributional features beyond the conditional mean, such as conditional quantiles and conditional value-at-risk (CVaR), which are better suited to capture downside risk and tail behavior [7, 8, 9]. More broadly, complex risk-sensitive criteria like Cumulative Prospect Theory (CPT) have also been recognized as meaningful in health-related decision making [10, 11]. Originating in economics, CPT combines a value function with probability distortion to represent asymmetric preferences over gains and losses together with nonlinear attitudes toward unlikely events [12].

At the same time, existing risk-sensitive ITR methods face two related challenges. First, they are typically criterion-specific: a method designed for one treatment criterion, such as a conditional quantile or CVaR objective, generally does not transfer directly to another. As a result, adapting treatment recommendations to different patient preferences may require redesigning and retraining a separate learning procedure for each new criterion, which can substantially increase modeling and computational cost in practice. Second, direct criterion-specific learning becomes especially difficult for more complex risk-sensitive objectives. This is particularly clear for CPT-type criteria, whose functional form involves nonlinear transformations of cumulative probabilities rather than a simple expectation of a pointwise loss. Related evidence also appears in other decision-learning settings, such as reinforcement learning and agents [13, 14, 15, 16]. Taken together, these observations suggest that the challenge is broader than any single criterion and arises more generally when treatment learning is tied to a specific risk-sensitive objective.

Problem description. These considerations motivate the main question of this paper: how can we learn risk-sensitive ITRs in a unified and flexible way when the relevant treatment criterion depends on the full conditional outcome distribution rather than only its mean? The challenge is not only to optimize a single pre-specified risk-sensitive criterion, but to develop a general approach that can support multiple treatment criteria and remain applicable when the target objective is difficult to optimize directly. Such a formulation would make it possible to compare treatment rules under different risk-sensitive objectives and to accommodate more complex criteria beyond the standard conditional mean-based setting.

Related work and our method. Our goal is to develop a unified framework for risk-sensitive ITR learning under the potential outcome framework. A natural starting point is that many treatment criteria of interest can be written as functionals of the conditional outcome distribution given patient covariates. This suggests a distribution-first strategy: first estimate the treatment-specific conditional outcome distribution, then obtain the target criterion by plug-in evaluation, and finally construct the treatment rule by comparing criterion values across treatments. This perspective is especially appealing when one wishes to compare treatment rules under different criteria or handle objectives that are difficult to optimize directly.

This view is supported by a broad literature on conditional distribution estimation. Classical approaches include kernel-based conditional distribution estimation [17], while more recent work has developed random forest-based methods for conditional quantile and distribution learning [18, 19, 20]. There is also growing interest in modern generative approaches to conditional sampling and distribution learning, including deep generative methods such as GCDS [21] and related neural density estimators [22]. Diffusion-based generative models, such as denoising diffusion probabilistic models (DDPMs) [23], offer another flexible approach to distribution learning. Recent work has further extended diffusion models to causal inference, such as DiffPO [24], which models potential outcome distributions while addressing treatment selection bias. Together, these methods provide increasingly rich options for estimating treatment-specific conditional outcome distributions.

To the best of our knowledge, unlike criterion-specific methods [2, 3, 4, 5, 6], there has been no work that explicitly proposes a unified framework for risk-sensitive ITR learning. The work closest to ours appears in offline policy assessment, where Huang et al. [25] studied plug-in estimation of Lipschitz criteria by first estimating the target policy’s outcome CDF and then analyzing how CDF estimation error propagates to criterion estimation error. However, their setting differs from ours in several aspects. First, they estimate the policy-induced marginal outcome distribution for policy assessment, whereas we focus on treatment- and covariate-specific conditional outcome distributions. Second, our goal is treatment recommendation, which requires treatment rule comparison and regret analysis rather than criterion estimation alone. Our work builds on this perspective but shifts the focus from criterion estimation to treatment recommendation. Another related work is Näf et al. [26], which develops a distributional forest-based estimator of conditional treatment effects. Its focus is distributional treatment effect estimation and inference rather than criterion-specific treatment rule construction.

Contributions. Our main contributions are as follows. (1) We formulate a distribution-first framework for risk-sensitive ITR learning to provide a unified way to learn treatment rules under multiple criteria and accommodate complex objectives that are difficult to handle by direct criterion-specific optimization. (2) We establish a theoretical analysis for this framework by linking the first-stage distribution estimation error to downstream criterion estimation and treatment regret in the ITR setting. (3) We empirically show that the proposed framework outperforms direct criterion-specific methods in multiple settings, and we further evaluate the framework on a real data application to illustrate a complete pipeline.

2 Distribution-First Risk-Sensitive ITR Learning

We observe i.i.d. samples {(Xi,Ai,Yi)}i=1n\{(X_{i},A_{i},Y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n}, where Xi∈𝒳⊆ℝpX_{i}\in\mathcal{X}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{p} is a vector of covariates, Ai∈𝒜={−1,+1}A_{i}\in\mathcal{A}=\{-1,+1\} is the treatment assignment, and Yi∈ℝY_{i}\in\mathbb{R} is the observed outcome, with larger values preferred. Let Yi​(a)Y_{i}(a) denote the potential outcome under treatment a∈𝒜a\in\mathcal{A}. We make the following standard identification assumptions[27].

Assumption 1 (Identification).

For each a∈𝒜a\in\mathcal{A}: (i) consistency, Y=Y⁡(A)Y=Y(A); (ii) unconfoundedness, Y⁡(a)⟂A|XY(a)\perp A\mid X; and (iii) positivity, there exists η>0\eta>0 such that η≤ℙ⁡(A=a∣X=x)≤1−η,∀x∈𝒳\eta\leq\mathbb{P}(A=a\mid X=x)\leq 1-\eta,\ \forall x\in\mathcal{X}.

Under Assumption 1, the treatment-specific conditional distribution of the potential outcome is identified by Fa(y∣x)=ℙ{Y(a)≤y∣X=x}=ℙ{Y≤y∣X=x,A=a}F_{a}(y\mid x)=\mathbb{P}\{Y(a)\leq y\mid X=x\}=\mathbb{P}\{Y\leq y\mid X=x,A=a\}. Let 𝒯\mathcal{T} be a real-valued criterion functional on distributions, with larger values preferred. We define the treatment-specific score Qa𝒯(x)=𝒯{Fa(⋅∣x)}Q_{a}^{\mathcal{T}}(x)=\mathcal{T}\{F_{a}(\cdot\mid x)\}, and the corresponding optimal individualized treatment rule π𝒯​(x)∈arg⁡maxa∈𝒜​Qa𝒯​(x)\pi_{\mathcal{T}}(x)\in\arg\max_{a\in\mathcal{A}}Q_{a}^{\mathcal{T}}(x). This formulation makes clear that the target of learning is the full treatment-specific conditional distribution, rather than only the conditional mean, whenever treatment choice depends on distributional features beyond expectation.

Our distribution-first framework proceeds in two stages shown in Algorithm 1. In Stage 1, we estimate the treatment-specific conditional distributions Fa(⋅∣x)F_{a}(\cdot\mid x) for a∈𝒜a\in\mathcal{A}. Let F^a(⋅∣x)\widehat{F}_{a}(\cdot\mid x) denote a generic first-stage estimator. The framework is agnostic to the particular conditional distribution learner; in our experiments, we consider kernel-based estimators, random forest-based estimators, and modern generative models, which are discussed in Section 2.2. In Stage 2, we evaluate the target treatment criterion by plug-in: Q^a𝒯(x)=𝒯{F^a(⋅∣x)}\widehat{Q}_{a}^{\mathcal{T}}(x)=\mathcal{T}\{\widehat{F}_{a}(\cdot\mid x)\}, and return the estimated treatment rule π^𝒯​(x)∈arg⁡maxa∈𝒜​Q^a𝒯​(x)\widehat{\pi}_{\mathcal{T}}(x)\in\arg\max_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\widehat{Q}_{a}^{\mathcal{T}}(x). This modular design allows the same first-stage estimate to support multiple downstream criteria without redesigning the learning procedure for each objective.

2.1 Treatment criteria

A main advantage of the proposed framework is that different treatment criteria can be evaluated from the same estimated conditional distribution. These criteria correspond to different notions of utility, risk sensitivity, and personal preference. In this paper, we focus on four representative criteria: the conditional mean, the conditional quantile, CVaR, and CPT.

Conditional mean. The mean criterion is defined by 𝒯mean{Fa(⋅∣x)}=𝔼{Y(a)∣X=x}\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{mean}}\{F_{a}(\cdot\mid x)\}=\mathbb{E}\{Y(a)\mid X=x\}. This is the standard objective in much of the classical ITR literature. It corresponds to risk-neutral decision making, in the sense that treatments are compared solely through their average outcomes. While natural and interpretable, the conditional mean criterion ignores variability, tail behavior, and asymmetry of the outcome distribution.

Conditional quantile. For τ∈(0,1)\tau\in(0,1), let Qτ​{Y⁡(a)∣X=x}=inf{y:Fa​(y∣x)≥τ}Q_{\tau}\{Y(a)\mid X=x\}=\inf\{y:F_{a}(y\mid x)\geq\tau\} denote the conditional τ\tau-quantile under treatment aa. The corresponding criterion is 𝒯Q,τ{Fa(⋅∣x)}=Qτ{Y(a)∣X=x}\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{Q},\tau}\{F_{a}(\cdot\mid x)\}=Q_{\tau}\{Y(a)\mid X=x\}. Quantile-based decision making focuses on a specific location of the outcome distribution rather than its average. When τ\tau is small, the criterion emphasizes lower-tail performance and yields a more conservative treatment rule.

Conditional value-at-risk (CVaR). For α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1), we define the lower-tail CVaR by CVaRα​{Y⁡(a)∣X=x}=1α​∫0αQu​{Y⁡(a)∣X=x}​𝑑u\mathrm{CVaR}_{\alpha}\{Y(a)\mid X=x\}=\frac{1}{\alpha}\int_{0}^{\alpha}Q_{u}\{Y(a)\mid X=x\}\,du. The associated criterion is 𝒯CVaR,α{Fa(⋅∣x)}=CVaRα{Y(a)∣X=x}\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{CVaR},\alpha}\{F_{a}(\cdot\mid x)\}=\mathrm{CVaR}_{\alpha}\{Y(a)\mid X=x\}. CVaR summarizes the average outcome over the worst α\alpha fraction of the conditional distribution. Compared with a single lower quantile, it captures the overall severity of adverse outcomes in the lower tail and is therefore a more informative measure of downside risk. In personalized treatment learning, CVaR is particularly relevant when severe but relatively rare unfavorable outcomes must be explicitly controlled.

Cumulative prospect theory (CPT). Unlike the previous criteria, CPT is designed to encode personal preferences under risk, including asymmetric attitudes toward gains and losses and nonlinear perception of probabilities. Let r⁡(x)r(x) be a reference point and define the centered outcome Z⁡(a)=Y⁡(a)−r⁡(x)Z(a)=Y(a)-r(x). We use the value function

u⁡(z)={u+​(z)=zη+,z≥0,−u−​(−z)=−λ​(−z)η−,z<0,u(z)=\begin{cases}u^{+}(z)=z^{\eta_{+}},&z\geq 0,\\[3.0pt] -u^{-}(-z)=-\lambda(-z)^{\eta_{-}},&z<0,\end{cases}

where λ>1\lambda>1 captures loss aversion, and η+,η−∈(0,1]\eta_{+},\eta_{-}\in(0,1] control diminishing sensitivity over gains and losses. Let Ga(⋅∣x)G_{a}(\cdot\mid x) denote the conditional distribution function of Z⁡(a)|X=xZ(a)\mid X=x. Given probability-weighting functions w+w^{+} and w−w^{-} for gains and losses, the CPT criterion is

𝒯CPT{Fa(⋅∣x)}=∫0∞w+(1−Ga(z∣x))du+(z)−∫0∞w−(Ga(−z∣x))du−(z).\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{CPT}}\{F_{a}(\cdot\mid x)\}=\int_{0}^{\infty}w^{+}\!\left(1-G_{a}(z\mid x)\right)\,du^{+}(z)-\int_{0}^{\infty}w^{-}\!\left(G_{a}(-z\mid x)\right)\,du^{-}(z).

CPT is useful when treatment choice should reflect not only statistical risk but also behavioral preference. Relative to above criteria, CPT can represent richer patient-specific attitudes, such as stronger aversion to losses than attraction to gains, or overweighting of small probabilities. This makes CPT particularly appealing for personalized medicine when patients or clinicians care about more nuanced risk–reward tradeoffs.

2.2 First-stage conditional distribution estimation

Our distribution-first framework is modular. Instead of designing a separate learner for each decision criterion, we first estimate the treatment-specific conditional outcome distribution and then evaluate downstream functionals by plug-in.

We consider three broad classes of first-stage estimators: kernel-based methods, random forest-based methods, and generative models. These three estimator classes represent distinct modeling principles for first-stage distribution learning. Kernel methods emphasize local smoothness and interpretability, random forest-based methods emphasize adaptive partitioning and robustness in heterogeneous tabular data, and generative models emphasize flexibility for complex conditional distributions. By studying all three within the same framework, we can assess whether the downstream gains of distribution-first decision learning are robust across substantially different first-stage estimators.

Kernel-based estimators. Kernel methods estimate the conditional distribution by locally weighting observations near the target covariate value. For treatment arm aa, a generic estimator is

F^a​(y∣x)=∑i=1nKh​(Xi−x)​ 1​(Ai=a)​ 1​(Yi≤y)∑i=1nKh​(Xi−x)​ 1​(Ai=a),\widehat{F}_{a}(y\mid x)=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}K_{h}(X_{i}-x)\,\mathbf{1}(A_{i}=a)\,\mathbf{1}(Y_{i}\leq y)}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}K_{h}(X_{i}-x)\,\mathbf{1}(A_{i}=a)},

with an analogous density estimator obtained by additional smoothing in yy.

The main appeal of kernel methods is their simplicity and interpretability [17]. They impose relatively weak structural assumptions and are natural when the conditional distribution varies smoothly with covariates, making them a useful baseline for distribution-first learning. Their main limitation is that performance can degrade quickly in moderate or high dimensions, where local neighborhoods become sparse and estimation becomes sensitive to the choice of metric and bandwidth.

Random Forest-based estimators. Forest-based methods replace fixed metric neighborhoods with data-adaptive neighborhoods learned through recursive partitioning. For a treatment-specific fit, or a joint fit whose weights are zero outside the queried treatment arm, the fitted forest induces nonnegative weights αi(a)​(x)\alpha_{i}^{(a)}(x) satisfying ∑i:Ai=aαi(a)(x)=1\sum_{i:A_{i}=a}\alpha_{i}^{(a)}(x)=1. The resulting estimator is

F^a(y∣x)=∑i:Ai=aαi(a)(x) 1(Yi≤y).\widehat{F}_{a}(y\mid x)=\sum_{i:A_{i}=a}\alpha_{i}^{(a)}(x)\,\mathbf{1}(Y_{i}\leq y).

This formulation is closely related to distributional random forests and their causal extensions [28, 18, 20]. The main advantage of this class is adaptivity. Forest methods can capture nonlinearities, interactions, and heterogeneous structure without relying on a fixed distance in the ambient covariate space. This makes them especially attractive for tabular settings with moderate or high-dimensional covariates, where only a subset of variables may be relevant. In addition, the learned weights provide a convenient representation of the full conditional distribution, which aligns naturally with our plug-in framework.

Generative models. A more flexible alternative is to model Y⁡(a)|X=xY(a)\mid X=x generatively and sample Y~a,1​(x),…,Y~a,M​(x)∼P^​{Y⁡(a)∣X=x}\widetilde{Y}_{a,1}(x),\ldots,\widetilde{Y}_{a,M}(x)\sim\widehat{P}\{Y(a)\mid X=x\}, then construct an empirical distribution. This class includes GANs, normalizing flows, variational models, and conditional diffusion models [29, 30, 31, 23, 32, 33, 24, 34]. The main strength of this class is expressive power. Generative models can in principle represent complex non-Gaussian, skewed, heavy-tailed, or multimodal conditional outcome distributions that may be difficult to capture with local smoothing or recursive partitioning. This makes them a natural candidate when the outcome law has substantial distributional complexity. At the same time, they typically require heavier computation, more tuning, and larger effective sample sizes for stable training.

A key point is that the best estimator for global distributional fit need not be the best estimator for downstream decision quality under a particular criterion. For example, a method that fits the center of the distribution well may still perform poorly for tail-sensitive objectives if it misses lower-tail behavior. For this reason, we evaluate first-stage estimators primarily through the treatment rules they induce, rather than viewing conditional distribution estimation as an end in itself.

3 Theoretical Properties

We establish a general error propagation guarantee for the proposed framework, connecting first-stage conditional distribution estimation error to downstream criterion estimation error and, ultimately, to treatment policy regret. Our focus is on a broad class of Hölder-continuous functionals of the treatment-specific conditional outcome distribution. This formulation covers the main criteria considered in this work under criterion-specific regularity conditions, including the conditional mean, quantile, mean-variance, CVaR, and CPT.

For any treatment rule π\pi, define V𝒯​(π)=𝔼⁡[Qπ⁡(X)𝒯​(X)],ℛ𝒯​(π)=V𝒯​(π𝒯)−V𝒯​(π)V_{\mathcal{T}}(\pi)=\mathbb{E}\!\left[Q_{\pi(X)}^{\mathcal{T}}(X)\right],\ \mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{T}}(\pi)=V_{\mathcal{T}}(\pi_{\mathcal{T}})-V_{\mathcal{T}}(\pi). Define en𝒯​(x)=maxa∈𝒜⁡|Q^a𝒯​(x)−Qa𝒯​(x)|e_{n}^{\mathcal{T}}(x)=\max_{a\in\mathcal{A}}|\widehat{Q}_{a}^{\mathcal{T}}(x)-Q_{a}^{\mathcal{T}}(x)|, and δn𝒯(x)=maxad𝒯{F^a(⋅∣x),Fa(⋅∣x)}\delta_{n}^{\mathcal{T}}(x)=\max_{a}d_{\mathcal{T}}\{\widehat{F}_{a}(\cdot\mid x),F_{a}(\cdot\mid x)\}. So correspondingly, we have en,∞𝒯=supx∈𝒳en𝒯​(x)e_{n,\infty}^{\mathcal{T}}=\sup_{x\in\mathcal{X}}e_{n}^{\mathcal{T}}(x) and δn,∞𝒯=supx∈𝒳δn𝒯​(x)\delta_{n,\infty}^{\mathcal{T}}=\sup_{x\in\mathcal{X}}\delta_{n}^{\mathcal{T}}(x). We first characterize how perturbations of the estimated conditional distribution propagate to the criterion value.

Assumption 2 (Hölder continuity).

There exist L𝒯>0L_{\mathcal{T}}>0, ϵ𝒯>0\epsilon_{\mathcal{T}}>0, and 0<ρ𝒯≤10<\rho_{\mathcal{T}}\leq 1 such that, uniformly over aa and xx, for every distribution GG satisfying d𝒯{G,Fa(⋅∣x)}≤ϵ𝒯,d_{\mathcal{T}}\{G,F_{a}(\cdot\mid x)\}\leq\epsilon_{\mathcal{T}}, we have

|𝒯(G)−𝒯{Fa(⋅∣x)}|≤L𝒯d𝒯{G,Fa(⋅∣x)}ρ𝒯.|\mathcal{T}(G)-\mathcal{T}\{F_{a}(\cdot\mid x)\}|\leq L_{\mathcal{T}}d_{\mathcal{T}}\{G,F_{a}(\cdot\mid x)\}^{\rho_{\mathcal{T}}}.

Here, L𝒯L_{\mathcal{T}} is a criterion-specific stability constant, ϵ𝒯\epsilon_{\mathcal{T}} specifies the neighborhood over which the stability condition holds, while ρ𝒯\rho_{\mathcal{T}} is the Hölder exponent characterizing the sensitivity of the criterion to local distributional perturbations. When ρ𝒯=1\rho_{\mathcal{T}}=1, the condition gives local Lipschitz stability, related to the CDF-based Lipschitz formulation of Huang et al. [25]. Allowing ρ𝒯<1\rho_{\mathcal{T}}<1 extends the framework to non-Lipschitz distributional criteria, including the CPT specification considered in this work. The semimetric d𝒯d_{\mathcal{T}} may be chosen according to the criterion and the underlying distribution class, and need not be common across different criteria. Verification of this condition for the criteria considered in this paper is provided in Appendix A.1.

Define the Hölder-induced score-error bound e¯n𝒯:=L𝒯​(δn,∞𝒯)ρ𝒯\bar{e}_{n}^{\mathcal{T}}:=L_{\mathcal{T}}\bigl(\delta_{n,\infty}^{\mathcal{T}}\bigr)^{\rho_{\mathcal{T}}}. Under Assumption 2, whenever δn,∞𝒯≤ϵ𝒯\delta_{n,\infty}^{\mathcal{T}}\leq\epsilon_{\mathcal{T}}, the uniform criterion estimation error satisfies

en,∞𝒯≤e¯n𝒯.e_{n,\infty}^{\mathcal{T}}\leq\bar{e}_{n}^{\mathcal{T}}.

Thus, e¯n𝒯\bar{e}_{n}^{\mathcal{T}} summarizes how first-stage distribution estimation error propagates through the criterion-specific Hölder stability condition.

Theorem 1 (Baseline policy regret).

The plug-in treatment rule satisfies ℛ𝒯​(π^𝒯)≤2​en,∞𝒯\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{T}}(\widehat{\pi}_{\mathcal{T}})\leq 2e_{n,\infty}^{\mathcal{T}}. Under Assumption 2, if δn,∞𝒯≤ϵ𝒯\delta_{n,\infty}^{\mathcal{T}}\leq\epsilon_{\mathcal{T}}, then ℛ𝒯​(π^𝒯)≤2​e¯n𝒯\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{T}}(\widehat{\pi}_{\mathcal{T}})\leq 2\bar{e}_{n}^{\mathcal{T}}.

Theorem 1 establishes a direct link between first-stage conditional distribution estimation and the quality of the resulting treatment rule. A sharper guarantee is available when little probability mass lies near the treatment decision boundary. Let Q⋆𝒯​(x)=maxa∈𝒜⁡Qa𝒯​(x)Q_{\star}^{\mathcal{T}}(x)=\max_{a\in\mathcal{A}}Q_{a}^{\mathcal{T}}(x), and define the gap to the best strictly suboptimal treatment by Δ𝒯(x)=mina:Qa𝒯​(x)<Q⋆𝒯​(x){Q⋆𝒯(x)−Qa𝒯(x)}\Delta_{\mathcal{T}}(x)=\min_{a:\,Q_{a}^{\mathcal{T}}(x)<Q_{\star}^{\mathcal{T}}(x)}\left\{Q_{\star}^{\mathcal{T}}(x)-Q_{a}^{\mathcal{T}}(x)\right\}, with Δ𝒯​(x)=+∞\Delta_{\mathcal{T}}(x)=+\infty if all treatments are optimal.

Assumption 3 (Margin condition).

There are t0>0t_{0}>0 and a nondecreasing Ψ𝒯:[0,t0]→[0,1]\Psi_{\mathcal{T}}:[0,t_{0}]\to[0,1], with Ψ𝒯​(t)→0\Psi_{\mathcal{T}}(t)\to 0 as t↓0t\downarrow 0, such that

ℙX{Δ𝒯(X)≤t}≤Ψ𝒯(t),0<t≤t0.\mathbb{P}_{X}\{\Delta_{\mathcal{T}}(X)\leq t\}\leq\Psi_{\mathcal{T}}(t),\qquad 0<t\leq t_{0}.

The function Ψ𝒯\Psi_{\mathcal{T}} characterizes the probability mass near the treatment decision boundary, with smaller values corresponding to fewer covariate values for which a strictly suboptimal treatment is nearly optimal. This condition encompasses the standard margin or low-noise condition used to obtain fast rates in plug-in classification and policy learning[35, 36]. In comparison, existing direct-learning approaches obtain sharper rates under method-specific structural conditions, such as approximation-error, sparsity, or function-class assumptions [3, 9].

Theorem 2 (Boundary-refined policy regret).

Under Assumptions 2-3, if δn,∞𝒯≤ϵ𝒯\delta_{n,\infty}^{\mathcal{T}}\leq\epsilon_{\mathcal{T}} and 2​e¯n𝒯≤t02\bar{e}_{n}^{\mathcal{T}}\leq t_{0}, then ℛ𝒯​(π^𝒯)≤2​e¯n𝒯​Ψ𝒯​(2​e¯n𝒯)\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{T}}(\widehat{\pi}_{\mathcal{T}})\leq 2\bar{e}_{n}^{\mathcal{T}}\Psi_{\mathcal{T}}\bigl(2\bar{e}_{n}^{\mathcal{T}}\bigr).

Theorems 1 and 2 separate criterion stability from decision-boundary behavior. The quantity e¯n𝒯\bar{e}_{n}^{\mathcal{T}} summarizes the propagation of distribution estimation error through the criterion, while Ψ𝒯​(2​e¯n𝒯)\Psi_{\mathcal{T}}(2\bar{e}_{n}^{\mathcal{T}}) provides the boundary-dependent refinement of the baseline bound. Detailed verification for specific criteria, conditional distribution estimators, and explicit convergence-rate consequences under additional assumptions, is provided in Appendix A.

4 Simulations

We conduct simulation studies to evaluate the proposed framework. Throughout, we consider binary randomized trials with equal treatment assignment probabilities. We compare our methods with several representative baselines, including ℓ1\ell_{1}-PLS [3], RWL [5], CQR [37, 8], and the direct ℓ2\ell_{2}-CVaR method of Qi et al. [9]. Within our distribution-first framework, we further compare several first-stage conditional distribution estimators, including Kernel, Distributional Random Forest (DRF), Conditional DDPM, and GCDS. All results are based on 100 Monte Carlo replications. Kernel, ℓ1\ell_{1}-PLS, RWL, and the direct ℓ2\ell_{2}-CVaR method use cross-validation for tuning; other methods use prespecified or separately selected hyperparameters as provided in Appendix B. Across settings, the outcome is generated as Y=1+X1+X2+A​δ​(𝐗)+ϵY=1+X_{1}+X_{2}+A\delta(\mathbf{X})+\epsilon. We report four main metrics: Mean,Q0.1,CVaR0.1,CVaR0.25,Err.\texttt{Mean},\ Q_{0.1},\ \mathrm{CVaR}_{0.1},\mathrm{CVaR}_{0.25},\ \texttt{Err}. Here Mean measures overall policy value, and Err measures decision error relative to the oracle rule. We also report Q0.1Q_{0.1}, CVaR0.1\mathrm{CVaR}_{0.1}, and CVaR0.25\mathrm{CVaR}_{0.25} to assess lower-tail performance, since the proposed framework is intended to support risk-sensitive decision making. In particular, Q0.1Q_{0.1} captures a lower-tail threshold, whereas CVaR0.1\mathrm{CVaR}_{0.1} summarizes the average outcome among the worst 10%10\% of cases. These are standard downside-risk summaries and are especially informative in heavy-tailed settings [38, 9]. In the tables, for criterion-specific competitors, each row evaluates one native-trained rule under all reported criteria; for Kernel, DRF, Conditional DDPM, and GCDS, each Value/Err pair uses the plug-in rule targeting its column criterion.

Overall, our framework shows competitive performance among criterion-specific methods, especially when the outcome distribution skews from baseline settings. Among the candidate first-stage estimators, DRF is the most reliable overall choice.

4.1 Distribution Shift Examples

We first examine robustness under distribution shift, following the setup of Qi et al. [9]. In both shifted settings, we use δ⁡(𝐗)=X1−X2+X3\delta(\mathbf{X})=X_{1}-X_{2}+X_{3}, with n=200n=200 and p=20p=20. In the covariate shift setting, the training covariates are generated from Xj∼0.7​N​(0,1)+0.3​LogNormal​(0,2),X_{j}\sim 0.7\,N(0,1)+0.3\,\mathrm{LogNormal}(0,2), whereas the test covariates follow Xj∼N⁡(0,1)X_{j}\sim N(0,1); the noise remains ε∼N⁡(0,1)\varepsilon\sim N(0,1) for both training and test samples. In the outcome shift setting, both training and test covariates follow Unif⁡([−1,1]p)\mathrm{Unif}([-1,1]^{p}), while the training noise is generated from ε∼0.7​N​(0,1)+0.3​LogNormal​(0,2),\varepsilon\sim 0.7\,N(0,1)+0.3\,\mathrm{LogNormal}(0,2), and the test noise follows ε∼N⁡(0,1)\varepsilon\sim N(0,1). For simplicity, we only compare Kernel and ℓ2\ell_{2}-CVaR in this subsection. This follows Qi et al. [9], where ℓ2\ell_{2}-CVaR is already the strongest criterion-specific robust competitor in this experiment.

Table 1 shows that Kernel is consistently more stable than ℓ2\ell_{2}-CVaR under both types of shift. The main reason might be that our method depends more directly on the conditional distribution, instead of a single criterion-specific training objective, and therefore is more robust when the training and test environments differ. The internal comparison within the framework is also informative. In the outcome shift scenario, Kernel plug-in rules based on risk-sensitive criteria substantially outperform the mean-based rule, reflecting that lower-tail criteria are less affected by the heavy-tailed training noise than the conditional mean.

4.2 Comparison Across Outcome Regimes

We evaluate the proposed framework further via three additional examples. In the main text, we focus on dimension p=10p=10 and n=1000n=1000 since this setting is close to our real data, with additional results deferred to Appendix B. Xj​∼iid​Unif​[−1,1]X_{j}\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}\mathrm{Unif}[-1,1]. The testing sample size is 10,000. The experimental settings below are from [9]:

Setting 1 (linear Gaussian): δ⁡(X)=X1−X2+X3,ε∼N⁡(0,1)\delta(X)=X_{1}-X_{2}+X_{3},\ \varepsilon\sim N(0,1).

Setting 2 (nonlinear Gaussian): δ⁡(X)=ς⁡(X1)​ς​(X2)−c0,ς⁡(x)=1+1/(1+exp⁡{−20​(x−1/3)}),ε∼N⁡(0,1)\delta(X)=\varsigma(X_{1})\varsigma(X_{2})-c_{0},\ \varsigma(x)=1+1/(1+\exp\{-20(x-1/3)\}),\ \varepsilon\sim N(0,1), with c0=1.87c_{0}=1.87.

Setting 3 (heavy-tail): δ⁡(X)=X1−X2+X3,log⁡ε∼N⁡(0,22)\delta(X)=X_{1}-X_{2}+X_{3},\ \log\varepsilon\sim N(0,2^{2}).

Setting 1 is the standard sparse linear Gaussian benchmark and is oracle for both ℓ1\ell_{1}-PLS and CQR. Setting 2 is used to test adaptation to nonlinear decision boundary. Setting 3 introduces heavy right-tailed lognormal noise, which is used to assess the robustness of different ITRs and is also oracle for CQR. Because ε\varepsilon is independent of (X,A)(X,A) in Settings 1–3, the two treatment-specific conditional outcome distributions differ only by a location shift. All criteria considered here are monotone with respect to first-order stochastic dominance, so they share the same oracle rule sign⁡{δ⁡(X)}\operatorname{sign}\{\delta(X)\}. These settings therefore assess how accurately each method recovers this common rule under different outcome regimes. Appendix B.4 considers a treatment-interactive design in which the optimal rule genuinely depends on the criterion.

The results are summarized in Tables 2–4. Overall, our framework shows competitive performance among criterion-specific methods. In Setting 1, the proposed framework remains competitive even in this favorable regime for classical linear baselines. Within the distribution-first family, Conditional DDPM performs best, followed by GCDS and DRF. In Setting 2, DRF becomes the strongest method among all competitors, showing its ability to adapt to nonlinear treatment heterogeneity. Conditional DDPM and GCDS remain competitive with criterion-specific methods. In Setting 3, GCDS, Kernel, and DRF all clearly outper- form the other baselines beyond oracle CQR. In the distribution-first family, DRF has the highest Q0.1Q_{0.1} and CVaR0.1\mathrm{CVaR}_{0.1} Values, whereas Kernel has the highest CVaR0.25\mathrm{CVaR}_{0.25} Values and the lowest Err at all four tail criteria. The linear mean-based baselines deteriorate sharply in this regime. Since all criteria share the same oracle rule here, this deterioration reflects the sensitivity of squared-loss estimation to heavy right-tailed noise, whereas quantile- and CVaR-based plug-in rules are more robust to such noise. Together with the treatment-interactive and higher-dimensional experiments in Appendix B, these results show that DRF is the most reliable first-stage estimator in most settings, whereas Kernel degrades quickly as pp grows and the generative estimators are less stable, with one GCDS run failing. We therefore recommend DRF as the default first-stage estimator and regard generative models as promising but exploratory.

5 Real data analysis

We evaluate the proposed framework on the ACTG175 HIV clinical trial, a randomized study comparing several antiretroviral regimens in HIV-infected adult[39]. We compare ZDV+ddI with ZDV+ZAL among 1,046 participants, and use the cohort and 12 baseline covariates supplied with Qi et al. [9]. The outcome is the change in CD4 count from baseline to follow-up with larger values preferred. All methods use the same 200 treatment-stratified 80/20 splits. The results show that our framework yields a more flexible treatment rule than the criterion-specific methods, while maintaining strong out-of-sample performance.

We compare ℓ1\ell_{1}-PLS, ℓ2\ell_{2}-CVaR(0.25), and CQR(0.25), with three policies derived from our distribution-first framework: DRF-Mean, DRF-CVaR(0.25), and DRF-CPT. For the proposed approach, we first estimate the conditional outcome distribution under each treatment arm using DRF, and then construct treatment rules by optimizing different decision criteria with respect to the estimated distribution. All learned policies are evaluated on held-out test sets using mean value, CVaR0.25\text{CVaR}_{0.25}, and CPT. We also report the proportion of subjects assigned to treatment 1 (ZDV+ddI) and runtime. CPT uses reference point zero (no CD4 change), with η+=η−=0.88\eta_{+}=\eta_{-}=0.88, λ=2.25\lambda=2.25, γ+=0.61\gamma_{+}=0.61, and γ−=0.69\gamma_{-}=0.69 [12]. This choice is natural in the present setting, where avoiding poor outcomes and accounting for asymmetric gain-loss preferences may both be clinically relevant.

Table 5 reports all three utilities for each fixed learned rule. DRF-Mean has the highest average held-out mean, while DRF-CPT has the highest average marginal CVaR and CPT among the six policies. DRF-CVaR also has a numerically higher average CVaR than the three baselines, but a lower average mean, illustrating a tradeoff between the evaluated utilities. The three DRF-based policies also produce meaningfully different treatment rates, indicating that different downstream criteria can lead to substantively different treatment recommendations even when they are based on the same estimated conditional outcome distribution. This illustrates the practical value of the distribution-first framework that once a flexible conditional distribution model is fitted, one can construct and compare treatment rules tailored to different decision objectives within a single unified pipeline.

Runtime includes split extraction, initialization, parameter selection where applicable, fitting, prediction, and held-out evaluation. The DRF time covers all three policies and their full cross-utility evaluations. The CVaR pipeline includes five-fold cross-validation over 11 regularization parameters, whereas DRF uses fixed settings without a tuning search. With the split-specific regularization parameter already selected, the separately timed post-selection CVaR workflow takes 1.849 [1.380, 8.533] seconds. Thus, DRF’s computational benefit is reusable distribution estimation across criteria, rather than uniformly faster single-criterion learning.

6 Discussion

We study risk-sensitive ITR learning through a distribution-first framework. The key idea is to first estimate the treatment-specific conditional outcome distribution and then construct the treatment rule by plug-in criterion evaluation. This yields a unified pipeline for multiple risk-sensitive criteria, including mean, quantile, CVaR, and CPT-type objectives. Our results support this perspective both theoretically and empirically. The theory provides a general error propagation result from first-stage distribution estimation to downstream criterion estimation and treatment regret. Empirically, performance depends on the outcome regime and first-stage estimator, while the treatment-interactive and real-data analyses illustrate criterion-dependent decisions using shared distribution estimates.

Several directions remain for future work. First, extending the distribution-first approach to doubly robust estimators is a potential next step, especially for observational settings. Second, the current theory focuses on Hölder-continuous criteria; sharper results for specific criteria may yield stronger and more interpretable guarantees. Third, our experiments suggest that gains from generative models depend on the outcome regime and target criterion. Future work should therefore investigate broader data types and response structures where generative models may be better matched to the underlying outcome distribution.

Appendix A Additional theoretical details

A.1 Verification of the Hölder Continuity Condition

Assumption 2 is formulated at the level of criterion stability and allows the semimetric d𝒯d_{\mathcal{T}} to depend on the distributional criterion and the underlying distribution class. The formulation is closely related to the CDF-based Lipschitz risk-functional framework of Huang et al. [25], which establishes plug-in stability for a broad class of Lipschitz functionals and verifies such properties for criteria including the mean, CVaR, variance, mean–variance, and CPT-type objectives. These results correspond to the special case ρ𝒯=1\rho_{\mathcal{T}}=1 of Assumption 2.

The Hölder formulation relaxes the global Lipschitz requirement in two directions. First, it requires stability only locally, which accommodates criteria such as quantiles that are not globally Lipschitz but are locally Lipschitz under standard regularity conditions around the target quantile. Second, it allows Hölder exponents (ρ𝒯<1\rho_{\mathcal{T}}<1), which accommodates functionals that are locally continuous but not Lipschitz. In particular, the Tversky–Kahneman probability distortions used in our CPT specification exhibit singular behavior near the probability endpoints and are generally not Lipschitz on [0,1]. We show below that these distortions are Hölder continuous, yielding a corresponding Hölder stability bound for the CPT functional.

These conditions are not interchangeable: for example, CDF sup-norm convergence on an unbounded support does not by itself control a mean or a tail average.

For CPT, the formal statement below uses a prespecified fixed reference point r0=0r_{0}=0, matching the ACTG175 analysis. . Since F⁡(qτ)=τF(q_{\tau})=\tau and f≥cτf\geq c_{\tau} almost everywhere on the specified neighborhood,

For CPT, write

pF+(z)=PF{v+(Y)>z},pF−(z)=PF{v−(Y)>z},p_{F}^{+}(z)=P_{F}\{v^{+}(Y)>z\},\qquad p_{F}^{-}(z)=P_{F}\{v^{-}(Y)>z\},

This remains true when vv has flat regions.

By the Hölder continuity of the probability distortions,

|w±​(pF±​(z))−w±​(pG±​(z))|≤L±​δρ±.|w_{\pm}(p_{F}^{\pm}(z))-w_{\pm}(p_{G}^{\pm}(z))|\leq L_{\pm}\delta^{\rho_{\pm}}.

|𝒯CPT​(F)−𝒯CPT​(G)|\displaystyle|\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{CPT}}(F)-\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{CPT}}(G)| ≤∫0M+|w+​(pF+​(z))−w+​(pG+​(z))|​𝑑z\displaystyle\leq\int_{0}^{M_{+}}|w_{+}(p_{F}^{+}(z))-w_{+}(p_{G}^{+}(z))|\,dz
+∫0M−|w−(pF−(z))−w−(pG−(z))|dz\displaystyle\quad+\int_{0}^{M_{-}}|w_{-}(p_{F}^{-}(z))-w_{-}(p_{G}^{-}(z))|\,dz
≤L+​M+​δρ++L−​M−​δρ−.\displaystyle\leq L_{+}M_{+}\delta^{\rho_{+}}+L_{-}M_{-}\delta^{\rho_{-}}.

Letting ρ=min⁡(ρ+,ρ−)\rho=\min(\rho_{+},\rho_{-}), and noting that 0≤δ≤10\leq\delta\leq 1, we have δρ+≤δρ,δρ−≤δρ\delta^{\rho_{+}}\leq\delta^{\rho},\delta^{\rho_{-}}\leq\delta^{\rho}. Thus,

|𝒯CPT​(F)−𝒯CPT​(G)|≤(L+​M++L−​M−)​δρ,|\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{CPT}}(F)-\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{CPT}}(G)|\leq(L_{+}M_{+}+L_{-}M_{-})\delta^{\rho},

which proves the claim. ∎

Lemma 1 (Hölder continuity of the standard CPT distortion).

For the commonly used Tversky–Kahneman distortion

wγ​(p)=pγ{pγ+(1−p)γ}1/γ,0<γ<1,w_{\gamma}(p)=\frac{p^{\gamma}}{\{p^{\gamma}+(1-p)^{\gamma}\}^{1/\gamma}},\qquad 0<\gamma<1,

the endpoint behavior is Hölder. With gain and loss exponents γ+\gamma_{+} and γ−\gamma_{-}, respectively, Proposition 1 uses ρ𝒯=min⁡(γ+,γ−)\rho_{\mathcal{T}}=\min(\gamma_{+},\gamma_{-}). More generally, for every 0<γ<10<\gamma<1, there is a finite CγC_{\gamma} such that

|wγ​(p)−wγ​(q)|≤Cγ​|p−q|γ,p,q∈[0,1].\left|w_{\gamma}(p)-w_{\gamma}(q)\right|\leq C_{\gamma}\left|p-q\right|^{\gamma},\qquad p,q\in[0,1].
Proof.

Let Dγ​(p)=pγ+(1−p)γD_{\gamma}(p)=p^{\gamma}+(1-p)^{\gamma}. Because Dγ​(p)≥1D_{\gamma}(p)\geq 1, direct differentiation on (0,1)(0,1) gives

wγ′(p)=Dγ(p)−1/γ−1[(γ−1)p2​γ−1+γpγ−1(1−p)γ+pγ(1−p)γ−1].w_{\gamma}^{\prime}(p)=D_{\gamma}(p)^{-1/\gamma-1}\left[(\gamma-1)p^{2\gamma-1}+\gamma p^{\gamma-1}(1-p)^{\gamma}+p^{\gamma}(1-p)^{\gamma-1}\right].

Since 0<p<10<p<1, the triangle inequality therefore gives

|wγ′​(p)|≤pγ−1+(1−p)γ−1.\left|w_{\gamma}^{\prime}(p)\right|\leq p^{\gamma-1}+(1-p)^{\gamma-1}.

For 0≤p<q≤10\leq p<q\leq 1, integration therefore yields

|wγ​(q)−wγ​(p)|≤1γ​[qγ−pγ+(1−p)γ−(1−q)γ].\left|w_{\gamma}(q)-w_{\gamma}(p)\right|\leq\frac{1}{\gamma}\left[q^{\gamma}-p^{\gamma}+(1-p)^{\gamma}-(1-q)^{\gamma}\right].

The subadditivity of tγt^{\gamma} implies that each bracketed difference is at most (q−p)γ(q-p)^{\gamma}. Thus the claimed bound holds with Cγ=2/γC_{\gamma}=2/\gamma on (0,1)(0,1), and continuity of wγw_{\gamma} extends it to the endpoints. ∎

Remark 1 (Unbounded outcomes).

For Gaussian, lognormal, or other unbounded outcomes, the bounded-support statements in Proposition 1 require either outcome clipping that is also used by the algorithm, or explicit tail and moment assumptions with a truncation remainder. Alternatively, a criterion-matched transport metric may be used: W1W_{1} controls the mean and lower-tail CVaR under the required integrability, whereas variance needs second-moment control (for example through W2W_{2} plus uniform moment conditions), and unbounded CPT needs conditions matched to the growth of its value function. CDF sup-norm convergence alone cannot control a mean when a vanishing amount of mass may move arbitrarily far into the tail. Consequently, the bounded-support CDF theory does not by itself cover the Gaussian or lognormal simulations.

A.2 Proofs of the Main Theoretical Results

We first establish a pointwise oracle inequality for the plug-in treatment rule, which directly yields Theorem 1 and serves as the key step in proving Theorem 2.

Lemma 2 (Pointwise oracle inequality).

For every xx,

0≤Q⋆𝒯​(x)−Qπ^𝒯​(x)𝒯​(x)≤2​en𝒯​(x).0\leq Q_{\star}^{\mathcal{T}}(x)-Q_{\widehat{\pi}_{\mathcal{T}}(x)}^{\mathcal{T}}(x)\leq 2e_{n}^{\mathcal{T}}(x).

≤|Q^a⋆𝒯​(x)−Qa⋆𝒯​(x)|+|Q^π^𝒯​(x)𝒯​(x)−Qπ^𝒯​(x)𝒯​(x)|\displaystyle\leq\left|\widehat{Q}_{a^{\star}}^{\mathcal{T}}(x)-Q_{a^{\star}}^{\mathcal{T}}(x)\right|+\left|\widehat{Q}_{\widehat{\pi}_{\mathcal{T}}(x)}^{\mathcal{T}}(x)-Q_{\widehat{\pi}_{\mathcal{T}}(x)}^{\mathcal{T}}(x)\right|
≤2​en𝒯​(x).\displaystyle\leq 2e_{n}^{\mathcal{T}}(x).

∎

By the definition of policy regret and Lemma 2,

ℛ𝒯​(π^𝒯)=𝔼X​[Q⋆𝒯​(X)−Qπ^𝒯​(X)𝒯​(X)]≤2​en,∞𝒯.\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{T}}(\widehat{\pi}_{\mathcal{T}})=\mathbb{E}_{X}\left[Q_{\star}^{\mathcal{T}}(X)-Q_{\widehat{\pi}_{\mathcal{T}}(X)}^{\mathcal{T}}(X)\right]\leq 2e_{n,\infty}^{\mathcal{T}}.

The following lemma gives a general transfer from pointwise criterion estimation error to policy regret under the local boundary-mass condition. It serves as the common basis for both Theorem 2 and the integrated-error extension below.

The main-text results connect uniform conditional distribution estimation error to policy regret through the Hölder stability condition. Independently of this distribution-to-score transfer, Lemma 3 also yields regret guarantees directly from integrated criterion estimation errors. We record these score-level consequences under the familiar polynomial special case of the boundary-mass condition.

Remark 2 (Interpretation and limiting cases).

When κ=0\kappa=0, the polynomial condition supplies no rate acceleration, and all displays reduce to the first-stage score rate. Under a hard gap, Ψ𝒯​(t)=0\Psi_{\mathcal{T}}(t)=0 for t<t0t<t_{0}, a uniformly accurate plug-in rule has zero regret once 2​mn,∞<t02m_{n,\infty}<t_{0}. Without any restriction on mass near the decision boundary, a score perturbation of size ε\varepsilon may change the selected treatment on a region with gaps of order ε\varepsilon, so a general improvement over order ε\varepsilon is impossible. This is the same role played by low-noise assumptions in classical plug-in classification [35].

A.3 Estimator-Specific Guarantees

A.3.1 A generic weighted conditional-CDF estimator

Both kernel smoothers and forest estimators can be written as weighted empirical CDFs. For a treatment aa, let ℐa={i:Ai=a}\mathcal{I}_{a}=\{i:A_{i}=a\}, and consider

F^a,W​(y∣x)=∑i∈ℐaWi,a​(x)​𝟏​(Yi≤y),Wi,a​(x)≥0,∑i∈ℐaWi,a​(x)=1.\widehat{F}_{a,W}(y\mid x)=\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{a}}W_{i,a}(x)\mathbf{1}(Y_{i}\leq y),\qquad W_{i,a}(x)\geq 0,\qquad\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{a}}W_{i,a}(x)=1. (5)

This definition is used on ℰn,A={ℐa≠∅ for all a}\mathcal{E}_{n,A}=\{\mathcal{I}_{a}\neq\varnothing\text{ for all }a\}; outside that event, set each unavailable-arm estimate to a prespecified fixed CDF belonging to the domain of 𝒯\mathcal{T}. Under overlap,

ℙ⁡(ℰn,Ac)≤2​(1−η)n⟶0.\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E}_{n,A}^{c})\leq 2(1-\eta)^{n}\longrightarrow 0.

All weighted-estimator statements below are proved on ℰn,A\mathcal{E}_{n,A}. For bookkeeping, set the weights, localization bias, and squared weight mass to arbitrary bounded values off this event. Its exponentially small probability leaves the unconditional OℙO_{\mathbb{P}} conclusions unchanged. Let ℋn\mathcal{H}_{n} contain all covariates, treatment labels, algorithmic randomization, structure-sample observations, and other information used to construct the weights, but not the estimation outcomes appearing in (5).

Assumption 4 (Global honesty for the estimation outcomes).

Conditionally on ℋn\mathcal{H}_{n}, the weights in (5) are fixed, and the estimation outcomes appearing in that equation are independent with

𝔼⁡[𝟏​(Yi≤y)∣ℋn]=Fa​(y∣Xi),i∈ℐa.\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{1}(Y_{i}\leq y)\mid\mathcal{H}_{n}]=F_{a}(y\mid X_{i}),\qquad i\in\mathcal{I}_{a}.

For kernels, Assumption 4 holds because the weights depend only on XiX_{i} and AiA_{i}. For forests, it holds for a global sample-splitting construction in which a structure sample builds all partitions and an independent estimation sample supplies the weighted outcomes. Standard per-tree honesty does not automatically imply Assumption 4 for the final aggregate weights, because one observation can be used for splitting in some trees and for leaf estimation in others. This fixed-weight conditional-independence requirement is therefore stronger than the per-tree honesty used in generalized forest constructions [19].

Define the oracle weighted target, localization bias, squared weight mass, and effective sample size:

Fa,W​(y∣x)\displaystyle F_{a,W}(y\mid x) =∑i∈ℐaWi,a​(x)​Fa​(y∣Xi),\displaystyle=\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{a}}W_{i,a}(x)F_{a}(y\mid X_{i}),
Ba,n​(x)\displaystyle B_{a,n}(x) =∑i∈ℐaWi,a​(x)​supy|Fa​(y∣Xi)−Fa​(y∣x)|,\displaystyle=\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{a}}W_{i,a}(x)\sup_{y}\left|F_{a}(y\mid X_{i})-F_{a}(y\mid x)\right|,

The exact decomposition

F^a,W−Fa=(F^a,W−Fa,W)+(Fa,W−Fa)\widehat{F}_{a,W}-F_{a}=(\widehat{F}_{a,W}-F_{a,W})+(F_{a,W}-F_{a}) (6)

separates stochastic fluctuation from localization bias.

On ℰn,A\mathcal{E}_{n,A}, under Assumption 4, for every fixed a,xa,x and every finite 1≤r<∞1\leq r<\infty, there is a constant Cr<∞C_{r}<\infty such that

(𝔼[supy|F^a,W(y∣x)−Fa,W(y∣x)|r|ℋn])1/r≤CrSa,n1/2(x).\left(\mathbb{E}\!\left[\left.\sup_{y}\left|\widehat{F}_{a,W}(y\mid x)-F_{a,W}(y\mid x)\right|^{r}\right|\mathcal{H}_{n}\right]\right)^{1/r}\leq C_{r}S_{a,n}^{1/2}(x). (7)

Consequently,

supy|F^a,W​(y∣x)−Fa​(y∣x)|=Oℙ​(Ba,n​(x)+Sa,n1/2​(x))\sup_{y}\left|\widehat{F}_{a,W}(y\mid x)-F_{a}(y\mid x)\right|=O_{\mathbb{P}}\!\left(B_{a,n}(x)+S_{a,n}^{1/2}(x)\right) (8)

conditionally on the weight construction.

Proof.

The bias part of (6) is bounded by Ba,n​(x)B_{a,n}(x). For the stochastic part, write

This proves (7), and (8) follows from (6). ∎

Let X∼PXX\sim P_{X} be independent of the training data, let

Conditional Markov’s inequality yields the stochastic order in (9); the localization bias is handled by the triangle inequality. ∎

Corollary 2 (Weighted estimator regret).

Suppose Assumption 2 holds with d𝒯=d∞d_{\mathcal{T}}=d_{\infty}. Assume additionally that there exists M𝒯<∞M_{\mathcal{T}}<\infty such that

en𝒯​(x)≤M𝒯e_{n}^{\mathcal{T}}(x)\leq M_{\mathcal{T}}

uniformly in xx, almost surely. Assume that all rate sequences used below converge to zero. Let 1≤q<∞1\leq q<\infty satisfy ρ𝒯​q≥1\rho_{\mathcal{T}}q\geq 1, and apply Theorem 3 with r=ρ𝒯​qr=\rho_{\mathcal{T}}q. Then

‖en𝒯‖Lq​(PX)=Oℙ​[{b¯n,ρ𝒯​q+s¯n,ρ𝒯​q}ρ𝒯].\left\lVert e_{n}^{\mathcal{T}}\right\rVert_{L_{q}(P_{X})}=O_{\mathbb{P}}\!\left[\{\bar{b}_{n,\rho_{\mathcal{T}}q}+\bar{s}_{n,\rho_{\mathcal{T}}q}\}^{\rho_{\mathcal{T}}}\right]. (10)

Without a margin condition, applying Theorem 3 with r=1r=1, Jensen’s inequality, and 0≤δn,W≤10\leq\delta_{n,W}\leq 1 gives

ℛ𝒯​(π^𝒯)=Oℙ​[{b¯n,1+s¯n,1}ρ𝒯].\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{T}}(\widehat{\pi}_{\mathcal{T}})=O_{\mathbb{P}}\!\left[\{\bar{b}_{n,1}+\bar{s}_{n,1}\}^{\rho_{\mathcal{T}}}\right]. (11)

Under (2) and 1<q<∞1<q<\infty,

ℛ𝒯​(π^𝒯)=Oℙ​[{b¯n,ρ𝒯​q+s¯n,ρ𝒯​q}ρ𝒯​q​(1+κ)/(q+κ)].\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{T}}(\widehat{\pi}_{\mathcal{T}})=O_{\mathbb{P}}\!\left[\{\bar{b}_{n,\rho_{\mathcal{T}}q}+\bar{s}_{n,\rho_{\mathcal{T}}q}\}^{\rho_{\mathcal{T}}q(1+\kappa)/(q+\kappa)}\right]. (12)

A uniform-in-xx analogue requires a separate entropy or complexity condition for {Wa​(x):x∈𝒳}\{W_{a}(x):x\in\mathcal{X}\} and does not follow by setting q=∞q=\infty in the finite-rr integrated theorem.

Proof.

Write δn=δn,W\delta_{n}=\delta_{n,W}. On {δn(X)≤ϵ𝒯}\{\delta_{n}(X)\leq\epsilon_{\mathcal{T}}\}, Assumption 2 gives

en𝒯​(X)≤L𝒯​δn​(X)ρ𝒯.e_{n}^{\mathcal{T}}(X)\leq L_{\mathcal{T}}\delta_{n}(X)^{\rho_{\mathcal{T}}}.

‖en𝒯‖Lq​(PX)q\displaystyle\left\lVert e_{n}^{\mathcal{T}}\right\rVert_{L_{q}(P_{X})}^{q} ≤L𝒯q𝔼X[δn(X)ρ𝒯​q]+M𝒯qℙX{δn(X)>ϵ𝒯}\displaystyle\leq L_{\mathcal{T}}^{q}\mathbb{E}_{X}\!\left[\delta_{n}(X)^{\rho_{\mathcal{T}}q}\right]+M_{\mathcal{T}}^{q}\mathbb{P}_{X}\{\delta_{n}(X)>\epsilon_{\mathcal{T}}\}
≤(L𝒯q+M𝒯q​ϵ𝒯−ρ𝒯​q)​‖δn‖Lρ𝒯​q​(PX)ρ𝒯​q.\displaystyle\leq\left(L_{\mathcal{T}}^{q}+M_{\mathcal{T}}^{q}\epsilon_{\mathcal{T}}^{-\rho_{\mathcal{T}}q}\right)\left\lVert\delta_{n}\right\rVert_{L_{\rho_{\mathcal{T}}q}(P_{X})}^{\rho_{\mathcal{T}}q}.

A.3.2 Kernel conditional-CDF estimation

For Kh​(u)=h−p​K​(u/h)K_{h}(u)=h^{-p}K(u/h), consider the local-constant estimator

F^aK​(y∣x)=∑i=1nKh​(Xi−x)​𝟏​(Ai=a)​𝟏​(Yi≤y)∑i=1nKh​(Xi−x)​𝟏​(Ai=a).\widehat{F}_{a}^{K}(y\mid x)=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}K_{h}(X_{i}-x)\mathbf{1}(A_{i}=a)\mathbf{1}(Y_{i}\leq y)}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}K_{h}(X_{i}-x)\mathbf{1}(A_{i}=a)}. (13)

If the denominator is zero, define the estimate to be a prespecified fixed CDF belonging to the domain of 𝒯\mathcal{T}. The proof below shows that this fallback is unused uniformly on 𝒳0\mathcal{X}_{0} with probability tending to one.

Assumption 5 (Uniform kernel conditions).

The following conditions hold.

  1. 1.

    𝒳0⊂𝒳\mathcal{X}_{0}\subset\mathcal{X} is compact and ℙX​(X∈𝒳0)=1\mathbb{P}_{X}(X\in\mathcal{X}_{0})=1. The support is regular enough that the population kernel denominator is uniformly positive as specified below.

  2. 2.

    For each aa, the joint design density ga​(x)=fX​(x)​ea​(x)g_{a}(x)=f_{X}(x)e_{a}(x) is bounded above, and, for some cD,h0>0c_{D},h_{0}>0,

    infa∈𝒜,x∈𝒳00<h≤h0∫K⁡(v)​ga​(x+h​v)​𝟏​(x+h​v∈𝒳0)​𝑑v≥cD.\inf_{\begin{subarray}{c}a\in\mathcal{A},\,x\in\mathcal{X}_{0}\\ 0<h\leq h_{0}\end{subarray}}\int K(v)g_{a}(x+hv)\mathbf{1}(x+hv\in\mathcal{X}_{0})\,dv\geq c_{D}.

    A density bounded away from zero on a regular compact support is a standard sufficient condition.

  3. 3.

    KK is bounded, nonnegative, compactly supported, ∫K⁡(u)​𝑑u=1\int K(u)\,du=1, and its translates and dilations form a VC-type class. The corresponding product classes

    (X,A,Y)↦Kh​(X−x)​𝟏​(A=a)​𝟏​(Y≤y)(X,A,Y)\mapsto K_{h}(X-x)\mathbf{1}(A=a)\mathbf{1}(Y\leq y)

    and the denominator class without 𝟏​(Y≤y)\mathbf{1}(Y\leq y) are also assumed VC-type uniformly over (a,x,y,h)(a,x,y,h). This follows from standard permanence properties for product kernels of bounded variation and the threshold class.

  4. 4.

    For some 0<β≤10<\beta\leq 1 and LF<∞L_{F}<\infty,

    supa∈𝒜supy∈ℝ|Fa​(y∣x)−Fa​(y∣x′)|≤LF​‖x−x′‖2β\sup_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\sup_{y\in\mathbb{R}}\left|F_{a}(y\mid x)-F_{a}(y\mid x^{\prime})\right|\leq L_{F}\left\lVert x-x^{\prime}\right\rVert_{2}^{\beta} (14)

    for all x,x′∈𝒳0x,x^{\prime}\in\mathcal{X}_{0}.

  5. 5.

    h=hn→0h=h_{n}\to 0 and n​hnp/log⁡n→∞nh_{n}^{p}/\log n\to\infty.

The condition β≤1\beta\leq 1 corresponds to the local-constant estimator in (13). Exploiting smoothness beyond first order requires an appropriate higher-order or local-polynomial conditional-distribution estimator and its own shape-validity argument.

Theorem 4 (Uniform kernel conditional-CDF rate).

Under Assumptions 1 and 5,

maxa∈𝒜supx∈𝒳0supy∈ℝ|F^aK(y∣x)−Fa(y∣x)|=Oℙ(hnβ+log⁡nn​hnp).\max_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\sup_{x\in\mathcal{X}_{0}}\sup_{y\in\mathbb{R}}\left|\widehat{F}_{a}^{K}(y\mid x)-F_{a}(y\mid x)\right|=O_{\mathbb{P}}\!\left(h_{n}^{\beta}+\sqrt{\frac{\log n}{nh_{n}^{p}}}\right). (15)
Proof.

For each aa, write the numerator and denominator of (13), divided by nn, as Nn,a​(x,y)N_{n,a}(x,y) and Dn,a​(x)D_{n,a}(x). Their population counterparts are

N¯a,h​(x,y)\displaystyle\bar{N}_{a,h}(x,y) =∫x+h​v∈𝒳0K⁡(v)​ga​(x+h​v)​Fa​(y∣x+h​v)​𝑑v,\displaystyle=\int_{x+hv\in\mathcal{X}_{0}}K(v)g_{a}(x+hv)F_{a}(y\mid x+hv)\,dv,
D¯a,h​(x)\displaystyle\bar{D}_{a,h}(x) =∫x+h​v∈𝒳0K⁡(v)​ga​(x+h​v)​𝑑v.\displaystyle=\int_{x+hv\in\mathcal{X}_{0}}K(v)g_{a}(x+hv)\,dv.

The design-density lower bound and nonnegativity of KK imply infa,xD¯a,h​(x)>c>0\inf_{a,x}\bar{D}_{a,h}(x)>c>0. Moreover, (14) gives, uniformly in a,x,ya,x,y,

|N¯a,h​(x,y)/D¯a,h​(x)−Fa​(y∣x)|≤C​hβ.\left|\bar{N}_{a,h}(x,y)/\bar{D}_{a,h}(x)-F_{a}(y\mid x)\right|\leq Ch^{\beta}.

The VC-type assumption and the bounded, compactly supported kernel imply the uniform empirical-process bounds

supa,x,y|Nn,a​(x,y)−N¯a,h​(x,y)|\displaystyle\sup_{a,x,y}\left|N_{n,a}(x,y)-\bar{N}_{a,h}(x,y)\right| =Oℙ​(log⁡nn​hp),\displaystyle=O_{\mathbb{P}}\!\left(\sqrt{\frac{\log n}{nh^{p}}}\right),
supa,x|Dn,a​(x)−D¯a,h​(x)|\displaystyle\sup_{a,x}\left|D_{n,a}(x)-\bar{D}_{a,h}(x)\right| =Oℙ​(log⁡nn​hp).\displaystyle=O_{\mathbb{P}}\!\left(\sqrt{\frac{\log n}{nh^{p}}}\right).

More explicitly, the corresponding maximal inequality also contributes an envelope term of order log⁡n/(n​hp)\log n/(nh^{p}), which is dominated by the displayed square-root term under n​hp/log⁡n→∞nh^{p}/\log n\to\infty. These are standard uniform-in-bandwidth kernel empirical-process bounds [41]. The second display and n​hp/log⁡n→∞nh^{p}/\log n\to\infty ensure that the empirical denominator is uniformly bounded away from zero with probability tending to one. A ratio expansion and the uniform bias bound prove (15). This is the standard bias-stochastic structure for kernel conditional-distribution estimation [17]. ∎

rn,K=hnβ+log⁡nn​hnp.r_{n,K}=h_{n}^{\beta}+\sqrt{\frac{\log n}{nh_{n}^{p}}}.

ℛ𝒯​(π^𝒯K)\displaystyle\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{T}}(\widehat{\pi}_{\mathcal{T}}^{K}) =Oℙ(rn,Kρ𝒯)without a margin condition.\displaystyle=O_{\mathbb{P}}(r_{n,K}^{\rho_{\mathcal{T}}})\quad\text{without a margin condition}.
