ℛ𝒯​(π^𝒯K)=Oℙ​(rn,Kρ𝒯​(1+κ)).\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{T}}(\widehat{\pi}_{\mathcal{T}}^{K})=O_{\mathbb{P}}(r_{n,K}^{\rho_{\mathcal{T}}(1+\kappa)}).

The log-optimized bandwidth and resulting rate are

hn\displaystyle h_{n} ≍(log⁡nn)1/(2​β+p),\displaystyle\asymp\left(\frac{\log n}{n}\right)^{1/(2\beta+p)},
rn,K\displaystyle r_{n,K} ≍(log⁡nn)β/(2​β+p),\displaystyle\asymp\left(\frac{\log n}{n}\right)^{\beta/(2\beta+p)},
ℛ𝒯​(π^𝒯K)\displaystyle\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{T}}(\widehat{\pi}_{\mathcal{T}}^{K}) =Oℙ​[(log⁡nn)β​ρ𝒯​(1+κ)/(2​β+p)].\displaystyle=O_{\mathbb{P}}\!\left[\left(\frac{\log n}{n}\right)^{\beta\rho_{\mathcal{T}}(1+\kappa)/(2\beta+p)}\right].
Remark 3 (An interior-only kernel bound).

If Theorem 4 is proved only on 𝒳0\mathcal{X}_{0} but ℙ⁡(X∉𝒳0)>0\mathbb{P}(X\notin\mathcal{X}_{0})>0, it does not by itself imply a population regret rate. If all scores are bounded by M𝒯M_{\mathcal{T}}, one may instead add the explicit remainder

ℛ𝒯,𝒳0​(π^𝒯):=𝔼X​[{Q⋆𝒯​(X)−Qπ^𝒯​(X)𝒯​(X)}​𝟏​(X∈𝒳0)∣𝒟n],\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{T},\mathcal{X}_{0}}(\widehat{\pi}_{\mathcal{T}}):=\mathbb{E}_{X}\!\left[\{Q_{\star}^{\mathcal{T}}(X)-Q_{\widehat{\pi}_{\mathcal{T}}(X)}^{\mathcal{T}}(X)\}\mathbf{1}(X\in\mathcal{X}_{0})\mid\mathcal{D}_{n}\right],

and

ℛ𝒯​(π^𝒯)≤ℛ𝒯,𝒳0​(π^𝒯)+2​M𝒯​ℙ​(X∉𝒳0).\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{T}}(\widehat{\pi}_{\mathcal{T}})\leq\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{T},\mathcal{X}_{0}}(\widehat{\pi}_{\mathcal{T}})+2M_{\mathcal{T}}\mathbb{P}(X\notin\mathcal{X}_{0}).

For a sequence 𝒳0,n\mathcal{X}_{0,n}, the outside probability must be negligible relative to the claimed rate.

A.3.3 Distributional Random Forest

A forest conditional-CDF estimator has the form

F^aF(y∣x)=∑i:Ai=awi,a(x)𝟏(Yi≤y),wi,a(x)≥0,∑i:Ai=awi,a(x)=1.\widehat{F}_{a}^{F}(y\mid x)=\sum_{i:A_{i}=a}w_{i,a}(x)\mathbf{1}(Y_{i}\leq y),\qquad w_{i,a}(x)\geq 0,\qquad\sum_{i:A_{i}=a}w_{i,a}(x)=1. (16)

The formal result below covers treatment-specific fits, or a joint fit whose query at treatment aa produces weights that are zero outside arm aa and are normalized within that arm. A generic joint fit that assigns cross-arm weights requires a separate formulation on the joint (X,A)(X,A) space. Once estimated, the treatment-specific distributions can be reused for every downstream criterion without refitting criterion-specific objectives.

Suppose a global structure sample constructs all partitions and an independent estimation sample supplies the outcomes in (16). Then Assumption 4 holds and Theorem 3 applies. In particular, define

Ba,nF​(x)\displaystyle B_{a,n}^{F}(x) =∑i:Ai=awi,a(x)supy|Fa(y∣Xi)−Fa(y∣x)|,\displaystyle=\sum_{i:A_{i}=a}w_{i,a}(x)\sup_{y}\left|F_{a}(y\mid X_{i})-F_{a}(y\mid x)\right|,
Sa,nF​(x)\displaystyle S_{a,n}^{F}(x) =∑i:Ai=awi,a2(x).\displaystyle=\sum_{i:A_{i}=a}w_{i,a}^{2}(x).

If (14) holds, the more informative weighted localization bound is

Ba,nF(x)≤LF∑i:Ai=awi,a(x)‖Xi−x‖2β.B_{a,n}^{F}(x)\leq L_{F}\sum_{i:A_{i}=a}w_{i,a}(x)\left\lVert X_{i}-x\right\rVert_{2}^{\beta}.

This is preferable to the maximum radius of all observations with positive weight, which can be driven by a negligible forest weight.

Corollary 4 (Integrated forest regret).

Assume global sample splitting, binary treatment, CDF-supnorm criterion stability with exponent ρ𝒯\rho_{\mathcal{T}}, and the integrated weight controls below for the required finite values of rr:

‖maxa⁡Ba,nF‖Lr​(PX)=Oℙ​(b¯n,r),‖maxa⁡(Sa,nF)1/2‖Lr​(PX)=Oℙ​(s¯n,r).\left\lVert\max_{a}B_{a,n}^{F}\right\rVert_{L_{r}(P_{X})}=O_{\mathbb{P}}(\bar{b}_{n,r}),\qquad\left\lVert\max_{a}(S_{a,n}^{F})^{1/2}\right\rVert_{L_{r}(P_{X})}=O_{\mathbb{P}}(\bar{s}_{n,r}).

Then Corollary 2 gives an explicit regret bound. In particular, for a Lipschitz criterion and 1<q<∞1<q<\infty,

ℛ𝒯​(π^𝒯F)=Oℙ​[{b¯n,q+s¯n,q}q⁡(1+κ)/(q+κ)]\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{T}}(\widehat{\pi}_{\mathcal{T}}^{F})=O_{\mathbb{P}}\!\left[\{\bar{b}_{n,q}+\bar{s}_{n,q}\}^{q(1+\kappa)/(q+\kappa)}\right]

under (2); the no-margin bound is (11) with the forest weight quantities.

The published DRF theory of Ćevid et al. [20] establishes a fixed-xx polynomial rate for a conditional RKHS mean embedding under subsampling, honesty, regularity, symmetry, and random-splitting conditions. Renaming their subsample exponent to θ\theta, if sn≍nθs_{n}\asymp n^{\theta}, their Theorem 2 gives

‖μ^n​(x)−μ⁡(x)‖ℋ=Oℙ​(n−γDRF),γDRF=12​min⁡{1−θ,log⁡{(1−αreg)−1}log⁡(αreg−1)​πsplitp​θ},\left\lVert\widehat{\mu}_{n}(x)-\mu(x)\right\rVert_{\mathcal{H}}=O_{\mathbb{P}}(n^{-\gamma_{\mathrm{DRF}}}),\qquad\gamma_{\mathrm{DRF}}=\frac{1}{2}\min\!\left\{1-\theta,\frac{\log\{(1-\alpha_{\mathrm{reg}})^{-1}\}}{\log(\alpha_{\mathrm{reg}}^{-1})}\frac{\pi_{\mathrm{split}}}{p}\theta\right\},

for each fixed test point, under their assumptions on the design density, bounded kernel, conditional embedding, and forest construction. Here αreg\alpha_{\mathrm{reg}} and πsplit\pi_{\mathrm{split}} denote their tree-regularity and random-split constants. Their CDF and quantile corollaries establish consistency at appropriate continuity points. Those results do not directly provide a uniform-in-(x,y)(x,y) CDF sup-norm rate, nor do they establish automatic adaptation to an unknown intrinsic dimension.

Therefore, if the implementation uses standard per-tree honest DRF rather than the globally split construction above, define the pointwise criterion-matched distribution error by

δn,DRF𝒯(x):=maxa∈𝒜d𝒯{F^aDRF(⋅∣x),Fa(⋅∣x)}.\delta_{n,\mathrm{DRF}}^{\mathcal{T}}(x):=\max_{a\in\mathcal{A}}d_{\mathcal{T}}\!\left\{\widehat{F}_{a}^{\mathrm{DRF}}(\cdot\mid x),F_{a}(\cdot\mid x)\right\}.

A defensible generic assumption, for some finite 1≤r<∞1\leq r<\infty, is

‖δn,DRF𝒯‖Lr​(PX)=Oℙ​(rn,DRF),rn,DRF→0.\left\lVert\delta_{n,\mathrm{DRF}}^{\mathcal{T}}\right\rVert_{L_{r}(P_{X})}=O_{\mathbb{P}}(r_{n,\mathrm{DRF}}),\qquad r_{n,\mathrm{DRF}}\to 0.

This distribution-error condition does not by itself imply a regret rate. It must first be transferred to a score-error rate through the criterion-stability condition, after which Lemma 2 and Corollary 1 can be applied.

More explicitly, suppose Assumption 2 holds and that the bounded score-error condition used in Corollary 2 is satisfied. If r≥ρ𝒯r\geq\rho_{\mathcal{T}}, the same good-set/bad-set argument gives

‖en𝒯‖Lr/ρ𝒯​(PX)=Oℙ​(rn,DRFρ𝒯).\left\lVert e_{n}^{\mathcal{T}}\right\rVert_{L_{r/\rho_{\mathcal{T}}}(P_{X})}=O_{\mathbb{P}}(r_{n,\mathrm{DRF}}^{\rho_{\mathcal{T}}}).

Consequently,

ℛ𝒯​(π^𝒯DRF)=Oℙ​(rn,DRFρ𝒯)\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{T}}(\widehat{\pi}_{\mathcal{T}}^{\mathrm{DRF}})=O_{\mathbb{P}}(r_{n,\mathrm{DRF}}^{\rho_{\mathcal{T}}})

without a margin condition. If r>ρ𝒯r>\rho_{\mathcal{T}} and (2) holds, then

ℛ𝒯​(π^𝒯DRF)=Oℙ​(rn,DRFρ𝒯​r​(1+κ)/(r+ρ𝒯​κ)).\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{T}}(\widehat{\pi}_{\mathcal{T}}^{\mathrm{DRF}})=O_{\mathbb{P}}\!\left(r_{n,\mathrm{DRF}}^{\rho_{\mathcal{T}}r(1+\kappa)/(r+\rho_{\mathcal{T}}\kappa)}\right).

A separately established genuine uniform bound

supxδn,DRF𝒯​(x)=Oℙ​(rn,DRF)\sup_{x}\delta_{n,\mathrm{DRF}}^{\mathcal{T}}(x)=O_{\mathbb{P}}(r_{n,\mathrm{DRF}})

can instead be combined directly with Theorems 1–2. Under the polynomial margin condition, this gives

ℛ𝒯​(π^𝒯DRF)=Oℙ​(rn,DRFρ𝒯​(1+κ)).\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{T}}(\widehat{\pi}_{\mathcal{T}}^{\mathrm{DRF}})=O_{\mathbb{P}}\!\left(r_{n,\mathrm{DRF}}^{\rho_{\mathcal{T}}(1+\kappa)}\right).

The rate rn,DRFr_{n,\mathrm{DRF}} should not be replaced by a closed-form intrinsic-dimension expression unless that localization result is separately proved for the actual forest construction.

Remark 4 (Uniform forest bounds need weight-class complexity).

Pointwise control through Ba,nF​(x)B_{a,n}^{F}(x) and Sa,nF​(x)S_{a,n}^{F}(x) does not automatically yield a supremum over xx. A uniform result additionally requires a complexity bound for the collection of weight vectors indexed by xx. For example, if a conditional entropy or log-cardinality ℓn\ell_{n} controls that class, a typical high-level uniform CDF bound has the form

supa,x,y|F^aF​(y∣x)−Fa​(y∣x)|=Oℙ​(bn+sn​ℓn),\sup_{a,x,y}\left|\widehat{F}_{a}^{F}(y\mid x)-F_{a}(y\mid x)\right|=O_{\mathbb{P}}\!\left(b_{n}+\sqrt{s_{n}\ell_{n}}\right),

where bnb_{n} bounds the uniform localization bias and sns_{n} bounds the uniform squared weight mass. Taking ℓn=O⁡(log⁡n)\ell_{n}=O(\log n) requires a separate complexity argument; it does not follow from honesty alone.

Appendix B Additional experiment details

B.1 Compute resource

All simulations were run on UNC’s Longleaf cluster. Non-generative methods were fit in R 4.5.0 (drf 1.3.1, quantreg 6.1, DynTxRegime 4.16, glmnet 4.1-10) with 8 CPU cores and 32 GB of memory per job. Conditional DDPM was trained on a single NVIDIA A100 (40 GB) GPU with PyTorch 2.6.0 (CUDA 12.4), and GCDS was run with 4 CPU cores and 32 GB of memory using TensorFlow 2.16.2; both generative pipelines were driven from R 4.4.0.

The treatment-interactive experiment was run locally on macOS using R 4.4.1. The ACTG175 evaluation and runtime measurements were performed on an Apple M3 Pro using R 4.4.1, with numerical-library and DRF thread counts set to one.

B.2 Full Experimental Results

Tables 6, 11, and 14 report all five criteria and all CQR and ℓ2\ell_{2}-CVaR training levels for the same 100 paired replications as the main tables. Higher-dimensional results with p=20,50,100,300p=20,50,100,300 are also reported below.

In Setting 1, ℓ1\ell_{1}-PLS has the highest Value and lowest Err among non-oracle methods for all reported criteria at p=20,50,100,300p=20,50,100,300. Within the distribution-first family, Conditional DDPM performs best at p=20p=20, whereas DRF performs best at p=50,100,300p=50,100,300. In Setting 2, DRF has the highest Value and lowest Err for all five criteria at p=20p=20. At p=300p=300, DRF has the highest Mean Value, while ℓ1\ell_{1}-PLS has the lowest Err for all criteria and the highest quantile and CVaR Values. Within the distribution-first family at p=300p=300, DRF has the highest Values and lowest mean-targeted Err, whereas GCDS has the lowest tail-targeted Err among its evaluable repetitions. All methods have 100 evaluable repetitions except GCDS in Setting 2 at p=300p=300, which has 99; the failure record and reporting protocol are described in Appendix B.5. Core code for the experiments is available at https://github.com/zhenf530/Distributio_Risk_ITR.

B.3 Discussion about GCDS

We further consider two additional scenarios that are more favorable to GCDS [21]. Since the goal here is internal method selection rather than external benchmarking, we mainly compare these models with DRF, which was the strongest distribution-first estimator in the earlier experiments. Setting 4 uses multiplicative non-Gaussian noise: Y=(1+X1+X2+A⁡(X1−X2+X3))​Z,Z=exp⁡(0.5​ε),Y=\bigl(1+X_{1}+X_{2}+A(X_{1}-X_{2}+X_{3})\bigr)\,Z,\ Z=\exp(0.5\varepsilon), where ε\varepsilon follows a two-component Gaussian mixture. Setting 5 uses a mix Gaussian distribution: Y|X,A∼0.5​N​(m⁡(X)+A​δ​(X)−2,0.52)+0.5​N​(m⁡(X)+A​δ​(X)+2,0.52).Y\mid X,A\sim 0.5\,N(m(X)+A\delta(X)-2,0.5^{2})+0.5\,N(m(X)+A\delta(X)+2,0.5^{2}).

Tables 15–18 show that the gains remain local. Under Setting 4, GCDS is only marginally better than DRF at p=10p=10, and this advantage disappears already at p=20p=20. Under Setting 5, GCDS has a clear advantage at p=10p=10, but this advantage again disappears at p=20p=20. Hence, even in scenarios designed to favor generative estimators, the advantage is limited and unstable. Combined with the earlier benchmark results, this leads us to a cautious view of generative estimators in the current tabular ITR problem: they are feasible within the distribution-first framework and may provide gains in selected scenarios, but their behavior is not stable enough to justify using them as default choices. Given their substantially higher training and tuning cost, we currently regard generative models as promising but still exploratory extensions.

B.4 Treatment-Interactive Outcome Distributions

To examine criterion-dependent treatment decisions, we adopt the treatment-interactive error design from Simulation Study II of Xiao, Zhang, and Lu (2019). Let X1,X2X_{1},X_{2} be independent Uniform⁡[−1,1]\mathrm{Uniform}[-1,1] variables, let B∼Bernoulli⁡(0.5)B\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(0.5) independently of XX, and generate

Y=\displaystyle Y={} 1+0.5sin{π(X1−X2)}+0.25(1+X1+2X2)2\displaystyle 1+0.5\sin\{\pi(X_{1}-X_{2})\}+0.25(1+X_{1}+2X_{2})^{2}
+(B−0.5)​θ⊤​X~+(1+B​d0​X12)​ϵ,\displaystyle+(B-0.5)\theta^{\top}\widetilde{X}+(1+Bd_{0}X_{1}^{2})\epsilon,

where X~=(1,X1,X2)⊤\widetilde{X}=(1,X_{1},X_{2})^{\top}, θ=(0.5,2,−1)⊤\theta=(0.5,2,-1)^{\top}, d0=5d_{0}=5, and ϵ∼Gamma⁡(shape=1,rate=1)−1\epsilon\sim\mathrm{Gamma}(\mathrm{shape}=1,\mathrm{rate}=1)-1 independently of (X,B)(X,B). The implementation uses A∈{−1,+1}A\in\{-1,+1\} with B=(A+1)/2B=(A+1)/2. We use p=2p=2, n=800n=800, 100 Monte Carlo replications, and an independent test sample of size 10,000 per replication. Treatment changes both the conditional location and scale.

Table 19 reports the criterion-matched comparisons for Mean, Q0.1Q_{0.1}, and CVaR0.1\mathrm{CVaR}_{0.1}. Conditional regret is the corresponding oracle value minus the learned-rule value. For the mean criterion, ℓ1\ell_{1}-PLS performs best among the reported methods, consistent with the linear mean treatment contrast. For Q0.1Q_{0.1} and CVaR0.1\mathrm{CVaR}_{0.1}, DRF performs best and Kernel shows similar tail-criterion gains. These results illustrate criterion-adaptive decision making with flexible distribution estimation in this nonlinear-tail setting.

B.5 Tuning and Preflight Diagnostics

Non-generative methods.

The following protocol applies to Settings 1–3 and their higher-dimensional extensions. Kernel selects a bandwidth shared by both treatment arms by ten-fold cross-validation over {0.15,0.20,0.25,0.30,0.40,0.50,0.70,0.90,1.20,1.50,2.00}\{0.15,0.20,0.25,0.30,0.40,0.50,0.70,0.90,1.20,1.50,2.00\}, minimizing the mean squared CDF prediction error at empirical outcome quantiles for 20 equally spaced probability levels in [0.1,0.9][0.1,0.9], using all covariates. ℓ1\ell_{1}-PLS selects its penalty along the glmnet path by ten-fold cross-validation, maximizing the summed validation-fold policy value. RWL uses a linear kernel and five-fold policy-value cross-validation over {2−10,…,20}\{2^{-10},\ldots,2^{0}\}. ℓ2\ell_{2}-CVaR uses the same grid with five-fold cross-validation, CQR initialization within each training fold, and its original validation score, which under μ=0\mu=0 is the mean outcome among validation observations whose treatment agrees with the learned rule; it is then refit on the full training sample. CQR fits linear quantile regression with treatment interactions at τ∈{0.1,0.25,0.5}\tau\in\{0.1,0.25,0.5\} without tuning. DRF uses 500 trees per treatment arm and otherwise the defaults of drf 1.3.1.

Generative methods.

Conditional DDPM and GCDS are tuned on independent pilot data. We measure predictive accuracy by the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS; lower is better) on factual validation outcomes, averaged within and then equally across treatment arms, and define skill=1−CRPSmodel/CRPSref\mathrm{skill}=1-\mathrm{CRPS}_{\mathrm{model}}/\mathrm{CRPS}_{\mathrm{ref}}, where the reference is the covariate-free empirical outcome distribution of the corresponding training arm. Each candidate is fit on five pilot datasets with two training seeds each, using treatment-stratified 80/20 training–validation splits and 512 generated draws per validation covariate and arm. A candidate is eligible if at least 9 of its 10 runs succeed and its scores are finite on all five datasets; Conditional DDPM additionally requires mean skill of at least −0.10-0.10. Conditional DDPM searches learning rates {10−4,2×10−4}\{10^{-4},2\times 10^{-4}\} and hidden widths {64,128}\{64,128\}, selecting by a one-standard-error rule that favors smaller networks, with standard errors computed across the five dataset-level averages. GCDS searches generator and discriminator learning rates in {5×10−4,10−3}×{10−4,5×10−4}\{5\times 10^{-4},10^{-3}\}\times\{10^{-4},5\times 10^{-4}\} and, since its candidates share one architecture, selects the eligible candidate with the lowest mean CRPS. Checkpoints are assessed every 100 epochs up to 2,000 for Conditional DDPM and every 500 iterations up to 7,500 for GCDS; the final budget is the median selected checkpoint of the chosen candidate, rounded to the checkpoint interval. Formal fits use the full training sample and this budget without further checkpoint selection. Test outcomes and oracle policies are not used for tuning.

Both methods use batch size 128. Conditional DDPM uses 200 diffusion steps, vv-prediction, a cosine noise schedule, EMA decay 0.999, and 50-step deterministic DDIM sampling. GCDS uses three-dimensional Gaussian noise, generator hidden width 50, discriminator hidden widths (50,25)(50,25), and five discriminator updates per generator update. Selected configurations are listed in Table 20.

Preflight check.

Before formal evaluation, each selected configuration was run 20 times with independent seeds and treatment-stratified 80/20 splits, using no formal test data. It passed if at least 19 runs completed with finite validation CRPS and the median skill was nonnegative. This check assesses execution reliability and predictive quality. Although our protocol originally required passing it before formal evaluation, we evaluated all configurations, including those that did not pass (Table 20), and report all replications without performance-based exclusion. In formal evaluation, all Conditional DDPM runs were evaluable. One of 1,000 GCDS runs (Setting 2, p=300p=300) failed a generated-sample collapse check and could not be evaluated, so the GCDS entries in Table 13 average over 99 replications. Some fitted policies are also degenerate: in Setting 2 at p=300p=300, DRF’s CVaR0.1 rule assigns treatment −1-1 to every test subject in all 100 replications (Err 0.499); Conditional DDPM’s mean-targeted rule is constant in 5 of 100 replications in Setting 1 at p=300p=300 and in 48 of 100 in Setting 2 at p=300p=300. All such results are retained in the reported tables.

NeurIPS Paper Checklist

  1. 1.

    Claims

  2. Question: Do the main claims made in the abstract and introduction accurately reflect the paper’s contributions and scope?

  3. Answer: [Yes]

  4. Justification: The abstract and introduction accurately summarize the paper’s main contributions: the distribution-first framework, the theoretical analysis, and the empirical comparisons. They also reflect the scope of the paper and the criteria considered.

  5. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the abstract and introduction do not include the claims made in the paper.

    • •

      The abstract and/or introduction should clearly state the claims made, including the contributions made in the paper and important assumptions and limitations. A [No] or [N/A] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers.

    • •

      The claims made should match theoretical and experimental results, and reflect how much the results can be expected to generalize to other settings.

    • •

      It is fine to include aspirational goals as motivation as long as it is clear that these goals are not attained by the paper.

  6. 2.

    Limitations

  7. Question: Does the paper discuss the limitations of the work performed by the authors?

  8. Answer: [Yes]

  9. Justification: The paper discusses several limitations, including the current focus on Hölder-continuous treatment criteria, the plug-in nature of the framework, and the dependence of generative-model gains on the outcome regime and target criterion. It also outlines corresponding future directions, such as doubly robust extensions, sharper theory for specific criteria, and broader data settings.

  10. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper has no limitation while the answer [No] means that the paper has limitations, but those are not discussed in the paper.

    • •

      The authors are encouraged to create a separate “Limitations” section in their paper.

    • •

      The paper should point out any strong assumptions and how robust the results are to violations of these assumptions (e.g., independence assumptions, noiseless settings, model well-specification, asymptotic approximations only holding locally). The authors should reflect on how these assumptions might be violated in practice and what the implications would be.

    • •

      The authors should reflect on the scope of the claims made, e.g., if the approach was only tested on a few datasets or with a few runs. In general, empirical results often depend on implicit assumptions, which should be articulated.

    • •

      The authors should reflect on the factors that influence the performance of the approach. For example, a facial recognition algorithm may perform poorly when image resolution is low or images are taken in low lighting. Or a speech-to-text system might not be used reliably to provide closed captions for online lectures because it fails to handle technical jargon.

    • •

      The authors should discuss the computational efficiency of the proposed algorithms and how they scale with dataset size.

    • •

      If applicable, the authors should discuss possible limitations of their approach to address problems of privacy and fairness.

    • •

      While the authors might fear that complete honesty about limitations might be used by reviewers as grounds for rejection, a worse outcome might be that reviewers discover limitations that aren’t acknowledged in the paper. The authors should use their best judgment and recognize that individual actions in favor of transparency play an important role in developing norms that preserve the integrity of the community. Reviewers will be specifically instructed to not penalize honesty concerning limitations.

  11. 3.

    Theory assumptions and proofs

  12. Question: For each theoretical result, does the paper provide the full set of assumptions and a complete (and correct) proof?

  13. Answer: [Yes]

  14. Justification: Each theoretical result is stated under explicit assumptions, and full proofs are provided in the appendix. The main text also summarizes the role of the assumptions and the resulting error propagation and regret bounds.

  15. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include theoretical results.

    • •

      All the theorems, formulas, and proofs in the paper should be numbered and cross-referenced.

    • •

      All assumptions should be clearly stated or referenced in the statement of any theorems.

    • •

      The proofs can either appear in the main paper or the supplemental material, but if they appear in the supplemental material, the authors are encouraged to provide a short proof sketch to provide intuition.

    • •

      Inversely, any informal proof provided in the core of the paper should be complemented by formal proofs provided in appendix or supplemental material.

    • •

      Theorems and Lemmas that the proof relies upon should be properly referenced.

  16. 4.

    Experimental result reproducibility

  17. Question: Does the paper fully disclose all the information needed to reproduce the main experimental results of the paper to the extent that it affects the main claims and/or conclusions of the paper (regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not)?

  18. Answer: [Yes]

  19. Justification: The paper specifies the simulation settings, evaluation criteria, competing methods, and the real-data analysis setup needed to reproduce the main empirical results. It also describes the first-stage estimators and the overall distribution-first pipeline used in each experiment.

  20. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments.

    • •

      If the paper includes experiments, a [No] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers: Making the paper reproducible is important, regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not.

    • •

      If the contribution is a dataset and/or model, the authors should describe the steps taken to make their results reproducible or verifiable.

    • •

      Depending on the contribution, reproducibility can be accomplished in various ways. For example, if the contribution is a novel architecture, describing the architecture fully might suffice, or if the contribution is a specific model and empirical evaluation, it may be necessary to either make it possible for others to replicate the model with the same dataset, or provide access to the model. In general. releasing code and data is often one good way to accomplish this, but reproducibility can also be provided via detailed instructions for how to replicate the results, access to a hosted model (e.g., in the case of a large language model), releasing of a model checkpoint, or other means that are appropriate to the research performed.

    • •

      While NeurIPS does not require releasing code, the conference does require all submissions to provide some reasonable avenue for reproducibility, which may depend on the nature of the contribution. For example

      1. (a)

        If the contribution is primarily a new algorithm, the paper should make it clear how to reproduce that algorithm.

      2. (b)

        If the contribution is primarily a new model architecture, the paper should describe the architecture clearly and fully.

      3. (c)

        If the contribution is a new model (e.g., a large language model), then there should either be a way to access this model for reproducing the results or a way to reproduce the model (e.g., with an open-source dataset or instructions for how to construct the dataset).

      4. (d)

        We recognize that reproducibility may be tricky in some cases, in which case authors are welcome to describe the particular way they provide for reproducibility. In the case of closed-source models, it may be that access to the model is limited in some way (e.g., to registered users), but it should be possible for other researchers to have some path to reproducing or verifying the results.

  21. 5.

    Open access to data and code

  22. Question: Does the paper provide open access to the data and code, with sufficient instructions to faithfully reproduce the main experimental results, as described in supplemental material?

  23. Answer: [Yes]

  24. Justification: The paper provides access to the code and specifies the data source, simulation data-generation process, sample settings, and experimental configurations for the main results.

  25. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that paper does not include experiments requiring code.

    • •

      Please see the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines (https://neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy) for more details.

    • •

      While we encourage the release of code and data, we understand that this might not be possible, so [No] is an acceptable answer. Papers cannot be rejected simply for not including code, unless this is central to the contribution (e.g., for a new open-source benchmark).

    • •

      The instructions should contain the exact command and environment needed to run to reproduce the results. See the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines (https://neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy) for more details.

    • •

      The authors should provide instructions on data access and preparation, including how to access the raw data, preprocessed data, intermediate data, and generated data, etc.

    • •

      The authors should provide scripts to reproduce all experimental results for the new proposed method and baselines. If only a subset of experiments are reproducible, they should state which ones are omitted from the script and why.

    • •

      At submission time, to preserve anonymity, the authors should release anonymized versions (if applicable).

    • •

      Providing as much information as possible in supplemental material (appended to the paper) is recommended, but including URLs to data and code is permitted.

  26. 6.

    Experimental setting/details

  27. Question: Does the paper specify all the training and test details (e.g., data splits, hyperparameters, how they were chosen, type of optimizer) necessary to understand the results?

  28. Answer: [Yes]

  29. Justification: The paper specifies the simulation settings, sample sizes, data splits, evaluation criteria, and the main implementation choices for each experiment. These details are sufficient to understand how the results were obtained.

  30. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments.

    • •

      The experimental setting should be presented in the core of the paper to a level of detail that is necessary to appreciate the results and make sense of them.

    • •

      The full details can be provided either with the code, in appendix, or as supplemental material.

  31. 7.

    Experiment statistical significance

  32. Question: Does the paper report error bars suitably and correctly defined or other appropriate information about the statistical significance of the experiments?

  33. Answer: [Yes]

  34. Justification: Simulation results are reported with Monte Carlo standard errors across replications. ACTG175 utilities and treatment rates are reported with standard deviations across 200 paired splits, and runtimes with medians and interquartile ranges; these descriptive summaries do not establish statistical significance.

  35. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments.

    • •

      The authors should answer [Yes] if the results are accompanied by error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests, at least for the experiments that support the main claims of the paper.

    • •

      The factors of variability that the error bars are capturing should be clearly stated (for example, train/test split, initialization, random drawing of some parameter, or overall run with given experimental conditions).

    • •

      The method for calculating the error bars should be explained (closed form formula, call to a library function, bootstrap, etc.)

    • •

      The assumptions made should be given (e.g., Normally distributed errors).

    • •

      It should be clear whether the error bar is the standard deviation or the standard error of the mean.

    • •

      It is OK to report 1-sigma error bars, but one should state it. The authors should preferably report a 2-sigma error bar than state that they have a 96% CI, if the hypothesis of Normality of errors is not verified.

    • •

      For asymmetric distributions, the authors should be careful not to show in tables or figures symmetric error bars that would yield results that are out of range (e.g., negative error rates).

    • •

      If error bars are reported in tables or plots, the authors should explain in the text how they were calculated and reference the corresponding figures or tables in the text.

  36. 8.

    Experiments compute resources

  37. Question: For each experiment, does the paper provide sufficient information on the computer resources (type of compute workers, memory, time of execution) needed to reproduce the experiments?

  38. Answer: [Yes]

  39. Justification: The appendix describes the compute environment used for the experiments, including the cluster setting, CPU/GPU usage, software environment, and the main factors affecting computational cost. It also clarifies that the reported compute corresponds to the experiments included in the paper.

  40. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments.

    • •

      The paper should indicate the type of compute workers CPU or GPU, internal cluster, or cloud provider, including relevant memory and storage.

    • •

      The paper should provide the amount of compute required for each of the individual experimental runs as well as estimate the total compute.

    • •

      The paper should disclose whether the full research project required more compute than the experiments reported in the paper (e.g., preliminary or failed experiments that didn’t make it into the paper).

  41. 9.

    Code of ethics

  42. Question: Does the research conducted in the paper conform, in every respect, with the NeurIPS Code of Ethics https://neurips.cc/public/EthicsGuidelines?

  43. Answer: [Yes]

  44. Justification: We have reviewed the NeurIPS Code of Ethics and are not aware of any aspect of this work that violates it. The paper uses standard simulation studies and a public clinical trial dataset, with no human-subject interaction or other special ethical concerns beyond those discussed in the paper.

  45. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the authors have not reviewed the NeurIPS Code of Ethics.

    • •

      If the authors answer [No] , they should explain the special circumstances that require a deviation from the Code of Ethics.

    • •

      The authors should make sure to preserve anonymity (e.g., if there is a special consideration due to laws or regulations in their jurisdiction).

  46. 10.

    Broader impacts

  47. Question: Does the paper discuss both potential positive societal impacts and negative societal impacts of the work performed?

  48. Answer: [No]

  49. Justification: The paper is primarily a foundational methodological study, and we do not identify an immediate direct path to societal harm from the proposed framework itself. The paper discusses its potential positive relevance to precision medicine.

  50. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that there is no societal impact of the work performed.

    • •

      If the authors answer [N/A] or [No] , they should explain why their work has no societal impact or why the paper does not address societal impact.

    • •

      Examples of negative societal impacts include potential malicious or unintended uses (e.g., disinformation, generating fake profiles, surveillance), fairness considerations (e.g., deployment of technologies that could make decisions that unfairly impact specific groups), privacy considerations, and security considerations.

    • •

      The conference expects that many papers will be foundational research and not tied to particular applications, let alone deployments. However, if there is a direct path to any negative applications, the authors should point it out. For example, it is legitimate to point out that an improvement in the quality of generative models could be used to generate Deepfakes for disinformation. On the other hand, it is not needed to point out that a generic algorithm for optimizing neural networks could enable people to train models that generate Deepfakes faster.

    • •

      The authors should consider possible harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended and functioning correctly, harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended but gives incorrect results, and harms following from (intentional or unintentional) misuse of the technology.

    • •

      If there are negative societal impacts, the authors could also discuss possible mitigation strategies (e.g., gated release of models, providing defenses in addition to attacks, mechanisms for monitoring misuse, mechanisms to monitor how a system learns from feedback over time, improving the efficiency and accessibility of ML).

  51. 11.

    Safeguards

  52. Question: Does the paper describe safeguards that have been put in place for responsible release of data or models that have a high risk for misuse (e.g., pre-trained language models, image generators, or scraped datasets)?

  53. Answer: [N/A]

  54. Justification: The paper does not release high-risk models, scraped datasets, or other resources with an obvious dual-use or misuse risk. It is a methodological study based on simulations and an existing clinical trial dataset.

  55. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper poses no such risks.

    • •

      Released models that have a high risk for misuse or dual-use should be released with necessary safeguards to allow for controlled use of the model, for example by requiring that users adhere to usage guidelines or restrictions to access the model or implementing safety filters.

    • •

      Datasets that have been scraped from the Internet could pose safety risks. The authors should describe how they avoided releasing unsafe images.

    • •

      We recognize that providing effective safeguards is challenging, and many papers do not require this, but we encourage authors to take this into account and make a best faith effort.

  57. Question: Are the creators or original owners of assets (e.g., code, data, models), used in the paper, properly credited and are the license and terms of use explicitly mentioned and properly respected?

      For existing datasets that are re-packaged, both the original license and the license of the derived asset (if it has changed) should be provided.

  65. Guidelines:
